say.text: A 35-year-old man is pulled out of a house fire. His voice is hoarse, there is soot in his mouth, and he has 30% burns. He is sitting up and talking in full sentences.
What is your first priority?

choices.label: Secure the airway now with early intubation
Calculate the Parkland volume and start fluids
Watch the airway; intubate only if stridor appears
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which problem gets worse hour by hour, and which one can close the airway. Then choose.
Yes. The **primary survey** (ABCDE) comes first, and the airway is part of it. Burn assessment belongs to the secondary survey.
Hoarseness and soot in the mouth are on the list for **early intubation**, before oedema builds.

choices.label: I am sure, skip the check

say.text: Tempting, because the burn numbers feel like the burn-specific job and seem urgent.
Not yet: the primary survey comes first, and the airway can close before the drip is even running.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so fix the order: burn numbers belong to the secondary survey.

choices.label: Why does the airway come first?

say.text: Tempting, because he is talking and looks safe for now.
Not yet: hoarseness and soot already call for **early intubation**, before the swelling closes the airway.

sure_note.text: You were sure the airway could wait. Stridor is one trigger on the list, not the start of the window.

say.text: The **primary survey** (ABCDE) runs first. Burn assessment and the fluid sum are done in the secondary survey.
An airway can swell shut as oedema builds, and it is easiest to secure before that. A fluid sum can wait a few minutes.
**Early intubation** is indicated before oedema develops, for stridor, hoarseness, deep facial burns or soot in the mouth.
Hoarseness and soot are features of inhalation injury. Waiting for stridor means waiting until the window has narrowed.
Two jobs in the first minutes: checking the airway, and estimating the burn's total body surface area. Which goes first, and why?

choices.label: The airway, because swelling can close it while numbers wait
Total body surface area first, since burn numbers set the fluids
Fluid volume first, so the drip starts on time
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which job can end a patient within minutes if it is left, not which one needs more arithmetic.
Tempting, because the surface area sets the whole fluid plan, so it feels like the first thing to fix.
Not yet: burn assessment belongs to the secondary survey, after the airway is safe.
Tempting, because a running drip looks like good resuscitation.
Not yet: the fluid volume is worked out after the primary survey, so the airway is checked first.
Yes. Swelling works on the airway now, while the surface area estimate is a secondary-survey task that can wait.
Why intubate now, in a patient who is speaking comfortably?

choices.label: Swelling builds over hours and can close the airway later
Airway swelling matters only once stridor or desaturation appears
Hoarseness proves lung injury, so a tube is needed now
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what the airway will do over the next several hours, not what it does right now.
Yes. Oedema builds over hours, so the window to pass a tube is widest now.
Partly right: hoarseness is a feature of inhalation injury, but it does not prove lung injury on its own.
The reason to act now is the swelling that is still to come.
Tempting, because stridor is the sign everyone is taught to watch for.
Not yet: soot and hoarseness already call for **early intubation**, before stridor appears.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so re-read the trigger list: stridor is one trigger, not the start of the window.
